title: “Monks, for a monk, those defilements that should be abandoned by direct knowledge have been abandoned by direct knowledge; those defilements that should be abandoned…
content: “Monks, for a monk, those defilements that should be abandoned by direct knowledge have been abandoned by direct knowledge; those defilements that should be abandoned by restraint have been abandoned by restraint … That monk is called one who lives restrained by the restraint of all defilements, who has cut off craving, has shed the fetters, has rightly penetrated conceit, and has made an end of suffering.”

title: “‘I will dwell contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and sorrow in the world.’ Thus, monk, you should…
content: “‘I will dwell contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and sorrow in the world.’ Thus, monk, you should train. Monk, when this concentration of yours is developed and cultivated in this way, then, monk, you should develop this concentration with initial and sustained thought; you should develop it without initial thought but with sustained thought; you should develop it without initial and sustained thought; you should develop it with rapture; you should develop it without rapture; you should develop it accompanied by pleasure; you should develop it accompanied by equanimity. Monk, when this concentration of yours is developed and cultivated in this way, then, monk, wherever you go, you will go at ease; wherever you stand, you will stand at ease; wherever you sit, you will sit at ease; wherever you lie down, you will lie down at ease.”

title: - “Venerable sir, right view — for what purpose is it?” - “Right view, Rādha, is for the purpose of disenchantment.” - “Venerable sir, disenchantment…
content: - “Venerable sir, right view — for what purpose is it?” - “Right view, Rādha, is for the purpose of disenchantment.” - “Venerable sir, disenchantment — for what purpose is it?” - “Disenchantment, Rādha, is for the purpose of dispassion.” - “Venerable sir, dispassion — for what purpose is it?” - “Dispassion, Rādha, is for the purpose of liberation.” - “Venerable sir, liberation — for what purpose is it?” - “Liberation, Rādha, is for the purpose of Nibbāna.” - “Venerable sir, Nibbāna — for what purpose is it?” - “Rādha, you have gone beyond the range of this question. For the purpose of entering Nibbāna, Rādha, is the holy life lived; Nibbāna is its final goal, Nibbāna is its end.”

title: “Aggivessana, pleasant feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. Aggivessana, painful feeling is…
content: “Aggivessana, pleasant feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. Aggivessana, painful feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. Aggivessana, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation.”

title: “Monks, those ascetics or brahmins in the past … in the future … in the present who regard whatever in the world is agreeable and…
content: “Monks, those ascetics or brahmins in the past … in the future … in the present who regard whatever in the world is agreeable and enticing as impermanent, as suffering, as not-self, as a disease, as fearful — they abandon craving. Those who abandon craving, abandon attachment. Those who abandon attachment, abandon suffering. Those who abandon suffering are freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that they are freed from suffering.”

title: Behold this decorated image — A heap of wounds, a collection of sores, Diseased, the object of many lustful thoughts, Nothing stable or permanent here.
content:
Behold this decorated image —
A heap of wounds, a collection of sores,
Diseased, the object of many lustful thoughts,
Nothing stable or permanent here.

title: “And for what benefit, monks, should a monk dwell with the perception of disgust toward the non-disgusting? ‘May greed not arise in me toward agreeable…
content: “And for what benefit, monks, should a monk dwell with the perception of disgust toward the non-disgusting? ‘May greed not arise in me toward agreeable states.’ For this benefit, monks, a monk should dwell with the perception of disgust toward the non-disgusting. And for what benefit, monks, should a monk dwell with the perception of non-disgust toward the disgusting? ‘May hatred not arise in me toward states that provoke hatred.’ For this benefit, a monk should dwell with the perception of non-disgust toward the disgusting. And for what benefit should a monk, abandoning both the non-disgusting and the disgusting, dwell equanimously, mindful and clearly comprehending? ‘May greed not arise in me toward agreeable states, wherever, however; may hatred not arise in me toward states that provoke hatred, wherever, however; may delusion not arise in me toward states that provoke delusion, wherever, however.’ For this benefit, monks, a monk, abandoning both the non-disgusting and the disgusting, dwells equanimously, mindful and clearly comprehending.”

title: “So too, Māgandiya, contact with sensual pleasures in the past was painful, very hot, very feverish; contact with sensual pleasures in the future will be…
content: “So too, Māgandiya, contact with sensual pleasures in the past was painful, very hot, very feverish; contact with sensual pleasures in the future will be painful, very hot, very feverish; contact with sensual pleasures in the present is painful, very hot, very feverish. And these beings who have not abandoned lust for sensual pleasures, being consumed by craving for sensual pleasures, burned by the fever of sensual pleasures, with corrupt faculties, perceive as pleasure that which is actually painful contact with sensual pleasures.”

title: The inner fetter and the outer fetter — Beings are entangled in these fetters. I ask Gotama about this: Who can escape these fetters? (The…
content:
The inner fetter and the outer fetter —
Beings are entangled in these fetters.
I ask Gotama about this:
Who can escape these fetters?

(The Blessed One):
One established in virtue, wise,
Developing mind and wisdom,
Ardent and discreet —
That monk can escape the fetters.
One who has abandoned greed,
Hatred, and ignorance,
The defilement-free arahant —
He has escaped the fetters.
Where name-and-form is destroyed
Without remainder,
Where the hindrance and perceptions of form are destroyed —
There the fetters are cut.

title: Elder Nitaka: The mind is like a rock, Standing firm, unmoved. Toward agreeable things, The mind has no desire. Toward things that disturb, The mind…
content:
Elder Nitaka:

The mind is like a rock,
Standing firm, unmoved.
Toward agreeable things,
The mind has no desire.
Toward things that disturb,
The mind is not disturbed.
One whose mind is thus developed —
From where can suffering come?

My mind is like a rock,
Standing firm, unmoved.
Toward agreeable things,
My mind has no desire.
Toward things that disturb,
My mind is not disturbed.
My mind is thus developed —
From where can suffering come to me?
